top.line: Refactoring the agent turns hope into enforced boundaries
top.para: One customer service mandate is built three ways and the same 62 fictional emails, sixteen hostile, run through each. The share of rules kept only by the model falls from 97% to 73% to 23%, and one run's reach falls from 38,000 records and unlimited refunds to one customer and 100 GBP per order.

s0.line: Only limits the agent cannot reach are controls
s0.para: Every design has a rule for every behaviour; what differs is who enforces it. Design 1 has 38 rules, 37 of them hope, while Design 2's harness cuts reach to 1,000 records, 5,000 GBP and 20 emails but is still 73% hope. Design 3 binds each run to one verified customer and is 23% hope.

s1.line: The mandate is twelve actions; the rest is excess
s1.para: Hollow Oak Home, an invented shop with 38,000 customers and about 1,400 support emails a week, wants routine mail answered automatically. The mandate includes refunds up to 100 GBP, a 10 GBP voucher once per order and 8,000 tokens per email. Barriers are none, expectation, setting or boundary, and only a boundary outside the grant is a control.

s2.line: One agent with two connectors is 97% hope
s2.para: A model wired to the mailbox with Gmail's broadest scope and a database role over every table gets a careful 38-rule policy. All but one rule is an expectation, so all sixteen hostile emails have an open path. It also uses about 35,000 tokens per email, breaking its own 8,000 budget every time.

s3.line: A harness cuts reach, but tool signatures keep hope
s3.para: Fourteen business tools replace the connectors, with no delete tool, a 250 GBP refund cap and a stop at twenty calls and 12,000 tokens. Reach falls to about 1,000 records and 5,000 GBP, and six of 22 rules become boundaries. But tools still take any customer, order or address, so 73% stays hope and fifteen hostile emails still get through.

s4.line: Narrow agents behind a code gateway leave little hope
s4.para: A deterministic gateway checks SPF, DKIM and DMARC and binds the run to one customer; intake, an orchestrator, five specialists, a controller and an analyst follow. Tools take no customer argument and carry the limits, including a 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker. 27 of 35 rules are boundaries, and tokens fall to about 4,400 per email.

s5.line: Two hostile emails still succeed inside the mandate
s5.para: A compromised real mailbox can redirect orders and claim refunds, and voucher farming abuses the damaged-goods route. Neither breaches a boundary, so the policy shows what to build next: an address confirmation link, a 250 GBP per customer cap over 30 days, and image-backed claims with two vouchers per 90 days. Tone stays sampled by a person.

s6.line: The policy is read again after every run
s6.para: For each rule the vault counts how often ordinary mail exercised it, how often hostile mail tested it, and whether a boundary or the model held. In Design 1 all 138 tests of 23 rules rested on the model; in Design 3, 52 of 85 were held by a boundary. Token budgets are rules too.

s7.line: The client sees eight promises and who keeps each
s7.para: All designs make the same eight promises, but Design 1 keeps none by a boundary, Design 2 one and Design 3 six. All three automate 91% of routine mail and save about 6,600 hours a year; they differ in a bad day's cost, from unbounded to one customer and the 2,000 GBP breaker.

s8.line: As reach falls, the policy itself gets smaller
s8.para: The policy shrinks not from carelessness but because it no longer has to forbid what the agent cannot do. Refactoring into many narrow tools is where most of the security comes from, and it is cheaper and easier to reason about. The policy shows where to refactor, where the risk is and when to stop.

s9.line: Write the mandate, mark enforcers, then bind the tools
s9.para: The steps: write the mandate, write the policy and mark each rule's enforcer, inspect tool signatures, bind tools to the verified sender, split by job and read the policy after every run. Drafted from Dinis Cruz's voice memo by Claude Opus 5.5 on 8 October 2026; the shop and simulation are fictional.
